content: Lactulose is typically prescribed in doses ranging from 7 to 60 grams per day, administered orally in divided doses. The dosage is titrated to achieve 2 to 3 soft stools per day. Aluminum hydroxide can reduce the effectiveness of lactulose due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution is advised, and monitoring is recommended. Similarly, calcium carbonate also decreases the effects of lactulose through pharmacodynamic antagonism, necessitating caution and monitoring. Both lactulose and deflazacort can lower serum potassium levels. This interaction requires careful monitoring. Dichlorphenamide and lactulose also decrease serum potassium levels, and their combined use can increase the toxicity of one another due to pharmacodynamic synergism. This combination may lead to metabolic acidosis, so therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is essential. Sodium bicarbonate reduces the effects of lactulose via pharmacodynamic antagonism, requiring caution and monitoring. Sodium citrate/citric acid also decreases lactulose's effects through a similar mechanism, necessitating the same precautions. Lactulose can enhance the effects of warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution and close monitoring are advised when these drugs are used together. Potential adverse effects of lactulose include dehydration, diarrhea, excessive bowel activity, hypernatremia, hypokalemia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, abdominal distension, belching, and flatulence. Patients with galactosemia should avoid lactulose due to its galactose content. Additionally, individuals with diabetes should be cautious, as lactulose contains lactose and galactose, which may affect blood sugar levels. Electrolyte imbalances should be monitored in patients using lactulose for more than six months or in those predisposed to electrolyte abnormalities. Concomitant use of other laxatives should be avoided, as this may lead to inadequate therapeutic response. Lactulose's effectiveness may also be reduced when taken with anti-infective agents. During pregnancy, lactulose is classified as Category B, indicating that controlled studies in pregnant women have not shown evidence of fetal risk. However, its safety during lactation is unknown, so caution is advised. Lactulose is a hyperosmotic agent that increases stool water content, softens stools, promotes peristalsis, and reduces blood ammonia concentrations. In cases of portal systemic encephalopathy, lactulose is metabolized by colonic bacteria into organic acids, acidifying colonic contents. This process inhibits the diffusion of ammonia back into the blood and enhances the conversion of ammonia (NH3) into ammonium (NH4+), which is excreted in the stool. Lactulose has a bioavailability of less than 3% and an onset of action within 24 to 48 hours. Absorbed lactulose is not metabolized, while unabsorbed lactulose is extensively metabolized by colonic bacteria into active metabolites, including lactic acid, formic acid, and acetic acid. Excretion occurs via urine (for absorbed lactulose) and feces and bile (for unabsorbed lactulose and its metabolites), though minimal amounts are excreted. Patients should take lactulose as directed by their healthcare provider, typically once daily for constipation. The solution can be mixed with fruit juice, water, milk, or a soft dessert to improve taste. Regular use at the same time each day is recommended for maximum benefit. It may take up to 48 hours to produce a bowel movement. Common side effects include gas, bloating, burping, stomach rumbling or pain, nausea, and cramps. Serious allergic reactions are rare. Patients should contact their healthcare provider for medical advice regarding side effects. Before using lactulose, patients should inform their healthcare provider of any allergies or medical conditions, particularly diabetes, as lactulose may affect blood sugar levels. Blood sugar should be monitored regularly, and results should be shared with the healthcare provider. In cases of overdose, immediate medical attention is required. U.S. residents can contact the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222, while Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. For long-term use, laboratory tests (e.g., blood mineral levels) should be conducted to monitor for potential complications. Patients should keep all medical and laboratory appointments. Missed doses should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is near the time of the next dose, in which case the missed dose should be skipped. The next dose should be taken at the regular time. Lactulose should be stored at room temperature, away from light, and should not be frozen. Medications should not be flushed down the toilet or poured into a drain unless instructed to do so. Expired or unused medication should be properly discarded. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about lactulose. Patients should consult their healthcare provider for complete information tailored to their specific health needs.
